```{r B34_reliability_splithalf, eval=FALSE}
  if (!any(is.finite(r)))
    stop("splithalf: every draw had fewer than ", min_features,
         " features estimable in both halves; the halves are too small",
         call. = FALSE)
  list(r = r[is.finite(r)], n_features = nf[is.finite(r)],
       B_used = sum(is.finite(r)), B = B,
       method = method, permuted = permute)
}

spearman_brown <- function(r) 2 * r / (1 + r)

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## splithalf_test(): the permutation test, with the null correctly specified
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## THE BUG THIS REPLACES. The first version drew one split per permutation and
## treated the resulting 200 values as the null distribution, then compared the
## MEDIAN of the observed splits against it. Those are not the same statistic.
## The observed median has averaged split-to-split noise away; the null had it
## all still in, which is why the observed permuted range came out at -0.47 to
## +0.47 while the observed splits sat in an IQR of 0.24 to 0.42. Comparing a
## median against a distribution of single draws inflates the p-value towards
## 1, and on the first run it returned p = 0.080 for a +0.349 observed against
## a -0.030 permuted centre -- a non-result manufactured by the mismatch.
##
## The statistic is T = median over splits of r. Its null distribution is
## obtained by permuting the labels and recomputing THE SAME T, splits and all.
## So the splits are nested inside each permutation.
##
## Cost is (1 + P) * S fits. The gene side is vectorised arithmetic and will
## take a couple of minutes at S = 50, P = 200. The proteome fits limma once
## per split, so start at S = 20, P = 100 and raise it only if p lands near the
## threshold.
splithalf_test <- function(effect_fun, resp, strata = NULL, S = 50, P = 200,
                           seed = 1, method = c("pearson", "spearman"),
                           min_features = 30) {
  method <- match.arg(method)
  resp <- droplevels(factor(resp))
  st <- if (is.null(strata)) factor(rep("all", length(resp)))
        else droplevels(factor(strata))
  stopifnot(length(st) == length(resp))

  obs_cells <- split(seq_along(resp), interaction(st, resp, drop = TRUE))
  bad <- obs_cells[lengths(obs_cells) < 4]
  if (length(bad))
    cat(sprintf("  %d sample(s) in %d stratum-arm cell(s) with < 4 members cannot be\n  split and are dropped from every draw, so the reliability below refers to a\n  fit on the %d samples that remain, not the full set\n",
                sum(lengths(bad)), length(bad),
                length(resp) - sum(lengths(bad))))

  one_split <- function(rr) {
    cells <- split(seq_along(rr), interaction(st, rr, drop = TRUE))
    cells <- cells[lengths(cells) >= 4]
    if (!length(cells)) return(NA_real_)
    a <- unlist(lapply(cells, function(ix) sample(ix, floor(length(ix) / 2))),
                use.names = FALSE)
    b <- setdiff(unlist(cells, use.names = FALSE), a)
    eA <- effect_fun(a, rr); eB <- effect_fun(b, rr)
    f <- intersect(names(eA), names(eB))
    if (length(f) < min_features) return(NA_real_)
    suppressWarnings(cor(eA[f], eB[f], method = method))
  }
  Tstat <- function(rr, keep = FALSE) {
    v <- vapply(seq_len(S), function(i) one_split(rr), numeric(1))
    out <- c(T = median(v, na.rm = TRUE), used = sum(is.finite(v)),
             sd_splits = sd(v, na.rm = TRUE))
    if (keep) attr(out, "splits") <- v
    out
  }
  shuffle_within <- function(r0) {
    out <- r0
    for (lv in levels(st)) {
      i <- which(st == lv)
      if (length(i) > 1) out[i] <- r0[sample(i)]
    }
    droplevels(out)
  }

  set.seed(seed)
  o <- Tstat(resp, keep = TRUE)
  if (!is.finite(o["T"]))
    stop("splithalf_test: no split had >= ", min_features,
         " features estimable in both halves", call. = FALSE)
  nul <- vapply(seq_len(P), function(p) Tstat(shuffle_within(resp))["T"],
                numeric(1))
  nul <- nul[is.finite(nul)]
  list(T_obs = unname(o["T"]), splits_used = unname(o["used"]), S = S,
       sd_splits = unname(o["sd_splits"]), r_splits = attr(o, "splits"),
       T_null = nul, P_used = length(nul), P = P,
       p = (1 + sum(nul >= o["T"])) / (length(nul) + 1),
       method = method)
}

spearman_brown <- function(r) 2 * r / (1 + r)

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## b34_report(): observed against the permuted null, and what it means
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
b34_report <- function(tst, label, se_rel = NULL) {
  q <- function(x, pr) unname(quantile(x, pr, na.rm = TRUE))
  To <- tst$T_obs; nl <- tst$T_null
  mc <- if (is.finite(tst$sd_splits))
          tst$sd_splits / sqrt(max(tst$splits_used, 1)) else NA_real_
  wide <- is.finite(mc) && sd(nl) > 2 * mc          # label-draw dominated null
  cat(sprintf("\n%s  (%s, median over %d splits, %d permutations)\n",
              label, tst$method, tst$splits_used, tst$P_used))
  cat(sprintf("  observed  T  %+.3f\n", To))
  cat(sprintf("  permuted  T  centre %+.3f, central 95%% %+.3f to %+.3f, SD %.3f\n",
              median(nl), q(nl, .025), q(nl, .975), sd(nl)))
  cat(sprintf("  permutation p  %.4f  (%d of %d permutations at or above; resolution %.4f)\n",
              tst$p, sum(nl >= To), tst$P_used, 1 / (tst$P_used + 1)))
  if (is.finite(mc))
    cat(sprintf("  spread: splits SD %.3f within a permutation, %.3f on the median of %d;\n          null SD %.3f -> %s\n",
                tst$sd_splits, mc, tst$splits_used, sd(nl),
                if (wide) "the null is label-draw structure, not split noise"
                else "the null is essentially split noise"))

  ## WHAT REPRODUCIBILITY MEANS HERE. A positive T says the two halves see the
  ## same across-feature pattern. It does NOT say that pattern is about
  ## response. If a random grouping of these patients also reproduces -- which
  ## is what a wide null means -- then the layer has strong patient-level
  ## structure that ANY two-group contrast picks up, and the response contrast
  ## has to be judged against that spread rather than against zero.
  if (To > 0) {
    cat(sprintf("  Spearman-Brown reliability  %+.2f  (of the reproducible pattern,\n    whatever it is about)\n",
                spearman_brown(To)))
    if (wide)
      cat("    No centre-corrected version is given: with a label-draw-dominated\n",
          "    null the non-response contribution to the OBSERVED value is not the\n",
          "    null's centre -- it is somewhere in the null's whole range -- so\n",
          "    subtracting a point value would not correct anything.\n", sep = "")
  } else {
    cat("  Spearman-Brown not reported: a non-positive T has no reliability\n",
        "  interpretation and the 2r/(1+r) form would return something that\n",
        "  looks like one.\n", sep = "")
  }
  if (!is.null(se_rel)) {
    cat(sprintf("  SE-based reliability on the same features  %+.2f  (effect SD %.3f, median SE %.3f)\n",
                se_rel["reliability"], sqrt(se_rel["var_obs"]), se_rel["median_se"]))
    d <- spearman_brown(max(To, 0)) - se_rel["reliability"]
    cat(sprintf("    the two methods %s (difference %+.2f)\n",
                if (abs(d) <= 0.2) "agree" else "disagree", d))
  }

  ## THE PRIMARY GATE IS p, AND THE FIRST VERSION LET TWO OTHER THINGS SPEAK
  ## OVER IT. On the clean 47-sample run T was +0.045 against a centre of
  ## -0.008 -- a difference of 0.053 against a 2 x Monte-Carlo bound of 0.050 --
  ## and that hair's breadth sent it down the "reproducible but not specific"
  ## branch, complete with a lecture on disattenuation, for a statistic that 78
  ## of 200 permutations matched or beat. A threshold built from Monte-Carlo
  ## error is far too fine when the null's own SD is 0.195. Judge "is there
  ## anything here" against the NULL's spread, not against the precision of the
  ## estimate.
  R <- spearman_brown(max(To, 0))
  cat("  VERDICT: ")
  if (tst$p > 0.05) {
    if (To <= median(nl) + 0.25 * sd(nl) || R < 0.2)
      cat("no response-specific reproducibility, and nothing much to\n",
          "    explain. T sits at the permuted centre: the halves share no\n",
          "    across-feature pattern that the response labels account for.\n",
          sep = "")
    else
      cat("reproducible, but NOT specific to response. T is well above the\n",
          "    permuted centre, so the halves do share a pattern -- but it is\n",
          "    inside the spread that random label draws produce, so the effect\n",
          "    variance is largely what any two-group split of these patients\n",
          "    would yield. That breaks the DISATTENUATION and not just the\n",
          "    p-value: rho_true = r_obs / sqrt(R_xx R_yy) needs R_xx to be the\n",
          "    reliability of the RESPONSE effect, and one inflated by\n",
          "    non-response structure makes the division wrong. Use a permutation\n",
          "    test of the cross-layer statistic, not the disattenuated estimate.\n",
          sep = "")
  } else if (R < 0.2)
    cat("response-specific but small. It clears the label-draw null, so it\n",
        "    is real, but the reliability is too low for a cross-layer correlation\n",
        "    to be estimable at any feature or set count here.\n", sep = "")
  else
    cat("response-specific and usable. It clears the label-draw null and the\n",
        "    reliability is workable. Take it into B31 and size the comparison on\n",
        "    the features both layers estimate.\n", sep = "")

  ## THE STANDARD-ERROR COMPARISON IS GATED ON p, which the first version also
  ## got wrong. With T not distinguishable from the null, both reliability
  ## estimates are consistent with zero true variance, and the gap between a
  ## Spearman-Brown of +0.09 and an SE-based -0.16 is arithmetic on two numbers
  ## that both mean "nothing". Announcing "the standard errors are likely
  ## overstated" from that is unfounded -- and at 327 features with no signal
  ## the SE-based estimate's own 95% range runs to -0.17, so -0.16 and -0.23
  ## are exactly what no signal looks like.
  if (!is.null(se_rel) && is.finite(se_rel["reliability"])) {
    if (tst$p > 0.05)
      cat("  ON THE STANDARD ERRORS: no comparison is made. With no reproducible\n",
          "    signal both estimates are consistent with zero true variance, and\n",
          "    their difference is not evidence about the standard errors.\n", sep = "")
    else {
      d <- R - se_rel["reliability"]
      if (d > 0.2)
        cat(sprintf(paste0("  ON THE STANDARD ERRORS: split-half exceeds the",
                           " SE-based figure by %+.2f,\n    so they are likely",
                           " overstated. Refit with moderated variances before",
                           "\n    using them in B31.\n"), d))
      else if (d < -0.2)
        cat("  ON THE STANDARD ERRORS: the SE-based figure exceeds split-half,\n",
            "    so var(effect) carries something the halves do not reproduce --\n",
            "    outliers or a few extreme features. Check the tail first.\n", sep = "")
      else
        cat("  ON THE STANDARD ERRORS: the two estimates agree, so they can be\n",
            "    used as they are.\n", sep = "")
    }
  }
  invisible(c(T_obs = To, T_null = median(nl), null_sd = sd(nl), p = tst$p,
              R_reproducible = spearman_brown(max(To, 0)),
              label_draw_dominated = wide))
}

cat(
"B34 loaded. With `mg`, MP, OP and v17's figure inputs in the session:\n\n",
"  source('B31_build_inputs.R'); source('B34_reliability_splithalf.R')\n\n",
"## ---- 1. gene side: is there anything reproducible there at all? --------\n",
"  mgw <- mg_fit_wide(mg)                       # all labelled metagenomes\n",
"  Lg  <- attr(mgw, 'matrix')[mgw$feature, , drop = FALSE]\n",
"  rg  <- attr(mgw, 'resp')\n",
"  tg  <- splithalf_test(mg_effect_fun(Lg), rg, S = 50, P = 200)\n",
"  b34_report(tg, 'metagenome, KO level', se_reliability(mgw$coef, mgw$se))\n\n",
"## ---- 2. proteome side: the positive control -----------------------------\n",
"  mps  <- intersect(colnames(MP), OP$d$sample)\n",
"  plex <- OP$d$Mixture[match(mps, OP$d$sample)]\n",
"  rp   <- OP$d$resp[match(mps, OP$d$sample)]\n",
"  Lp   <- as.matrix(MP[, mps]); Lp[Lp <= 0] <- NA_real_; Lp <- log(Lp)\n",
"  tp   <- splithalf_test(mp_effect_fun(Lp, plex), rp, strata = plex,\n",
"                         S = 20, P = 100)\n",
"  b34_report(tp, 'proteome, KO level')\n\n",
"## ---- 3. what changed: samples, or the feature set? ----------------------\n",
"## The wide gene fit keeps 4,209 features on ~67 samples where build_ko() kept\n",
"## 327 on 47. If its reliability differs from B31's, BOTH could be the cause,\n",
"## and the two are separable. Hold the feature set at B31's and refit wide:\n",
"  ko47 <- build_ko()\n",
"  f327 <- ko47$feature\n",
"  se_reliability(mgw$coef[mgw$feature %in% f327],\n",
"                 mgw$se[mgw$feature %in% f327])        # wide samples, B31 features\n",
"  se_reliability(ko47$mg_coef, ko47$mg_se)             # B31, both\n\n",
"## ---- 4. B31 again, on the wide gene fit ---------------------------------\n",
"  ko73 <- ko47 |> select(feature, mp_coef, mp_se) |>\n",
"    inner_join(mgw |> transmute(feature, mg_coef = coef, mg_se = se),\n",
"               by = 'feature')\n",
"  source('B31_crosslayer_attenuation.R')\n",
"  run_b31(list(KO_paired47 = ko47, KO_wide = ko73), out_dir = paths$out_dir)\n\n",
"READ 1 AND 2 TOGETHER. The proteome is the control: a response signal is\n",
"known to be there, so if ITS test comes back at chance the diagnostic is\n",
"broken and nothing should be concluded from the gene side. Only once the\n",
"proteome clears does a flat gene side mean anything.\n", sep = "")
```

## B35 — full space sets

the full-space family — 568 built, 565 scored — loaded, projected, and counted honestly

Source: `B35_full_space_sets.R`

```{r B35_full_space_sets, eval=FALSE}
## ============================================================================
## B35 — the full-space family (568 built, 565 scored), loaded, projected,
## and counted honestly
## ============================================================================
##
## A CORRECTION FIRST. I told you the survey memberships were not among v17's
## exports and that the family would have to be rebuilt. That was wrong. v17
## builds them in its own knit chunk -- written into the knit precisely because
## the earlier version "was built in a live session, which knitting does not
## leave behind" -- and saves them. The composition it prints is
##
##     KO COG Pfam KEGGmod KEGGpath reported TOTAL
##    108  21  244      86       79       30   568
##
## on the verified R1+R2+R3 universe of 5,106 Pittsburgh proteins. The scored
## run has 565 rather than 568 because that input was built in a session and
## lost 3 KO sets to an extra names(stat) intersect; v17 records this.
##
## THE TRAP, AND IT IS A REAL ONE. The chunk does this before saving:
##
##     SETS_P <- SETS_FULL        # "run_null.R reads SETS_P by name"
##
## so inside full_space/null_input.RData the object called SETS_P IS the
## 568-set family, not the 30 reported sets. That is why the B33 precheck saw
## 30: the session had the ordinary SETS_P from the main v17 path. It is also
## why this file loads into a fresh environment and never into the global one
## -- a bare load() here would silently replace the 30-set SETS_P that the
## reported-set analyses depend on, and nothing would complain.
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(tibble)
})

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## load_full_space(): the memberships, without clobbering anything
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
load_full_space <- function(dir = file.path(paths$out_dir, "full_space"),
                            expect_min = 500) {
  f <- file.path(dir, "null_input.RData")
  if (!file.exists(f))
    stop("load_full_space(): ", f, " not found.\n",
         "  It is written by v17's full-space chunk (section 13). Re-knit v17,",
         " or point\n  `dir` at the directory that chunk reported.",
         call. = FALSE)
  e <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
  load(f, envir = e)
  if (!exists("SETS_P", envir = e))
    stop("load_full_space(): no SETS_P in ", f, "; objects are ",
         paste(ls(e), collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
  S <- get("SETS_P", envir = e)
  if (length(S) < expect_min)
    stop(sprintf(paste0("load_full_space(): SETS_P in that file has only %d",
                        " sets. That is the 30-set\n  reported family, not the",
                        " full space -- this is the wrong file, or the chunk",
                        " ran\n  before the SETS_P <- SETS_FULL line."),
                 length(S)), call. = FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("load_full_space: %d sets from %s\n", length(S), f))
  print(layer_table(S))
  S
}

layer_table <- function(sets) {
  lay <- sub(":.*$", "", names(sets))
  lay[lay == names(sets)] <- "(unprefixed)"
  tibble(layer = lay, n = lengths(sets)) |>
    group_by(layer) |>
    summarise(sets = dplyr::n(), median_members = median(n),
              smallest = min(n), largest = max(n), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(sets))
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## project_report(): what the KO projection costs, per layer
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Run this instead of reading project_sets()'s single summary line, because
## the layers do not behave alike and one of them cannot survive at all:
##
##   KO (108 sets)  -- each is the proteins carrying ONE ortholog, so it
##                     projects to exactly one KO and dies at the size floor.
##                     Not a defect; the layer is simply not projectable, and
##                     it should be dropped by name so its loss is on the
##                     record rather than appearing as attrition.
##   KEGGmod, KEGGpath -- defined on KEGG upstream, so the projection is close
##                     to the identity and these should survive nearly intact.
##   COG (21)       -- broad categories, large, should all survive.
##   Pfam (244)     -- the floor is 10 PROTEINS, and a domain family's proteins
##                     often share few orthologs, so the small ones collapse
##                     below 10 KOs. Expect the heaviest losses here.
##   reported (30)  -- 21 survived when measured.
project_report <- function(sets, projected) {
  lay <- function(nm) { l <- sub(":.*$", "", nm); l[l == nm] <- "(unprefixed)"; l }
  ## project_sets() attaches a report over ALL input sets, including the ones
  ## it dropped at the floor. Use it: joining on the returned list instead
  ## would score a set that projected to 5 orthologs as 0, and the per-layer
  ## median KO count would then be wrong in exactly the layers that lost most.
  rep <- attr(projected, "report")
  if (is.null(rep)) {
    warning("project_report(): no `report` attribute; falling back to the ",
            "surviving sets only, so median_ko is biased upward.",
            call. = FALSE)
    rep <- tibble(set = names(sets), n_prot = lengths(sets),
                  n_ko = lengths(projected)[match(names(sets), names(projected))]) |>
      mutate(n_ko = coalesce(n_ko, 0L))
  }
  kept <- names(projected)
  t <- rep |> mutate(layer = lay(set), survived = set %in% kept)
  out <- t |> group_by(layer) |>
    summarise(sets_in = dplyr::n(), sets_out = sum(survived),
              median_prot = median(n_prot), median_ko = median(n_ko),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(kept = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sets_out / sets_in)) |>
    arrange(desc(sets_in))
  print(out)
  cat(sprintf("\n  %d of %d sets survive the projection\n",
              sum(t$survived), nrow(t)))
  if (any(t$layer == "KO" & t$survived))
    cat("  NOTE: KO-layer sets survived the projection. Check why -- a KO set\n",
        "  should collapse to a single ortholog. Either the members are not\n",
        "  proteins, or ko_primary is assigning several orthologs per protein.\n",
        sep = "")
  invisible(out)
}

drop_ko_layer <- function(sets) {
  k <- startsWith(names(sets), "KO:")
  if (any(k))
    cat(sprintf("drop_ko_layer: removing %d KO-layer sets (each projects to one\n  ortholog, so they cannot be scored in KO space)\n",
                sum(k)))
  sets[!k]
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## n_eff(): how many of those sets are actually independent
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## THIS IS THE PART THAT CHANGES THE DECISION, and the earlier interval-width
## simulation did not have it. Those numbers -- about 1.9 wide at 14 sets, 0.89
## at 150, 0.45 at 565 -- assumed independent sets. This family is nested by
## construction: Pfam domains inside orthologs inside modules inside pathways,
## and the 30 reported sets inside all of them. Two sets sharing most of their
## members give nearly the same pair of effect estimates, and a correlation
## computed over 300 such sets does not have 300 degrees of freedom.
##
## The permutation null absorbs part of this -- it widens the null spread
## correctly, because the same dependence is present in each draw. What it does
## NOT do is restore the sample size for the correlation's confidence interval.
## That needs the effective count.
##
## Computed as the participation ratio of the eigenvalues of the correlation
## matrix of the set indicator vectors over the ortholog universe,
##
##     n_eff = (sum lambda)^2 / sum lambda^2
##
## which equals m for orthogonal indicators and 1 when every set is the same
## set. It is a measure of the MEMBERSHIP redundancy, which is the thing under
## our control; it is not a substitute for the block bootstrap below, which is
## what should actually produce the interval.
n_eff <- function(sets, universe = NULL) {
  u <- if (is.null(universe)) sort(unique(unlist(sets))) else universe
  I <- vapply(sets, function(s) as.numeric(u %in% s), numeric(length(u)))
  keep <- apply(I, 2, sd) > 0
  if (sum(keep) < 2) stop("n_eff: fewer than two non-degenerate sets", call. = FALSE)
  I <- I[, keep, drop = FALSE]
  lam <- eigen(cor(I), symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
  lam <- lam[lam > 0]
  ne <- sum(lam)^2 / sum(lam^2)
  cat(sprintf("n_eff: %d sets over %d orthologs -> %.0f effective (%.0f%% redundant)\n",
              ncol(I), length(u), ne, 100 * (1 - ne / ncol(I))))
  ne
}

## Blocks for a bootstrap that respects the nesting: cluster sets by Jaccard
## distance and resample CLUSTERS, not sets. `h` is the distance at which to
## cut -- 0.5 groups sets sharing more than half their members.
set_blocks <- function(sets, h = 0.5) {
  m <- length(sets)
  u <- sort(unique(unlist(sets)))
  I <- vapply(sets, function(s) as.numeric(u %in% s), numeric(length(u)))
  inter <- crossprod(I)                       # |A and B|; needs numeric, not logical
  sz <- diag(inter)
  uni <- outer(sz, sz, "+") - inter
  J <- 1 - inter / pmax(uni, 1)
  cl <- stats::cutree(stats::hclust(stats::as.dist(J), method = "average"), h = h)
  cat(sprintf("set_blocks: %d sets -> %d blocks at Jaccard height %.2f (largest %d)\n",
              m, length(unique(cl)), h, max(table(cl))))
  split(names(sets), cl)
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## width_sim(): the expected spread of the answer, at the EFFECTIVE count
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## WHAT IS BEING SIZED, and I got this wrong once already. The first version of
## this function put a Fisher-z interval around the OBSERVED correlation, which
## gives 1.01 at 14 sets and 0.16 at 565 -- numbers that look far better than
## the ones quoted in Supplementary Note 8 and are the wrong target. The
## quantity B31 reports is the DISATTENUATED correlation, r_obs divided by the
## attenuation factor, and dividing by 0.37 multiplies the uncertainty by
## nearly three. Sizing the observed correlation would have made this look
## runnable at 150 sets when it is not.
##
## So the estimator itself is simulated: draw datasets at the given effective
## count and attenuation, disattenuate each one, and report the width of the
## central 95% of the resulting estimates. No interval theory, and the target
## is the published quantity.
##
##   n_eff    14    21    60   100   150   210   300   460   565
##   width  2.00  1.71  1.18  1.03  0.85  0.70  0.57  0.48  0.43
##
## (att = 0.37, true rho = 0.5. The width saturates at 2.00 because r_obs/att
## runs past the ends of [-1, 1] and is clamped.)
##
## TWO CORRECTIONS THIS TABLE FORCES ON WHAT I TOLD YOU EARLIER. "21 and even
## 60 sets are no better than 14" was too strong -- 60 is better (1.18 against
## 2.00) and still uninformative. And "roughly 150 sets before the permutations
## are worth running" was optimistic: 150 gives 0.85. Informative starts near
## 170, and nothing under about 400 is decisive.
##
## These widths are also a LOWER bound, because the simulation treats the
## attenuation factor as known. It is estimated from the two reliabilities,
## each of which has its own error, and that propagates into the division.
width_sim <- function(n_eff, att, rho = 0.5, B = 4000, seed = 1) {
  stopifnot(att > 0, att <= 1, n_eff >= 5)
  n <- max(5L, as.integer(round(n_eff)))
  s <- sqrt(1 / att - 1)
  set.seed(seed)
  est <- replicate(B, {
    t1 <- rnorm(n); t2 <- rho * t1 + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)
    r <- cor(t1 + rnorm(n, 0, s), t2 + rnorm(n, 0, s))
    max(-1, min(1, r / att))
  })
  qq <- unname(quantile(est, c(0.025, 0.975)))
  w <- diff(qq)
  cat(sprintf("width_sim: n_eff %d, attenuation %.2f, true rho %.2f\n", n, att, rho))
  cat(sprintf("  disattenuated estimate  median %+.2f, central 95%% %+.2f to %+.2f, width %.2f\n",
              median(est), qq[1], qq[2], w))
  cat(sprintf("  clamped at +/-1 in %.0f%% of draws\n", 100 * mean(abs(est) >= 1)))
  cat(if (w <= 0.4) "  VERDICT: decisive. Run it.\n"
      else if (w <= 0.8) "  VERDICT: informative, not decisive. Worth running if the\n    conclusion tolerates a band this wide.\n"
      else "  VERDICT: uninformative. The answer would be wider than the effect\n    being sought, and a wide interval reported as a result is how the\n    earlier version of this comparison went wrong.\n")
  cat("  (a lower bound: the attenuation factor is treated as known here)\n")
  invisible(c(width = w, lo = qq[1], hi = qq[2], median = median(est)))
}

cat(
"B35 loaded. Order of operations:\n\n",
"  source('B33_survey_crosslayer.R')   # project_sets(), ko_map()\n",
"  source('B35_full_space_sets.R')\n\n",
"  SF   <- load_full_space()                 # 568 sets, into no one's way\n",
"  SF   <- drop_ko_layer(SF)                 # 108 cannot be projected\n",
"  sets <- project_sets(SF, annot_new, min_size = 10)\n",
"  project_report(SF, sets)                  # per-layer, so the loss is visible\n\n",
"  ne   <- n_eff(sets)                       # the count that governs the interval\n",
"  width_sim(ne, att = 0.37)                 # att = sqrt(R_mg * R_mp) from the precheck\n\n",
"Only if width_sim says informative or better, go on to the precheck and the\n",
"permutations, with the proteome ranked through the protein route:\n\n",
"  mps  <- intersect(colnames(OP$a), OP$d$sample)\n",
"  plex <- OP$d$Mixture[match(mps, OP$d$sample)]\n",
"  mpf  <- ko_from_proteins(prot_ranker(protein_matrix(OP, mps), strata = plex))\n",
"  mgf  <- mg_ranker(mg)\n",
"  b33_precheck(sets, mpf(OP$d$resp[match(mps, OP$d$sample)]),\n",
"                     mgf(attr(mgf, 'resp')))\n\n",
"and give the interval from a bootstrap over set_blocks(sets), not from the\n",
"nominal count -- resampling individual sets would treat a Pfam family and the\n",
"pathway containing it as two independent observations.\n\n",
"RUN B34 FIRST. If the gene layer's split-half reliability is at its permuted\n",
"floor, every number above is moot: no set count rescues a layer with no\n",
"reproducible response structure, and this file would only produce a precise\n",
"zero.\n", sep = "")
```

## B36 — pathway coupling

does patient-specific coupling appear at PATHWAY level?

Source: `B36_pathway_coupling.R`

```{r B36_pathway_coupling, eval=FALSE}
## ============================================================================
## B36 — does patient-specific coupling appear at PATHWAY level?
## ============================================================================
##
## THE QUESTION, AND WHY IT IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM B31-B35. Those tried to
## correlate the two layers' RESPONSE CONTRASTS, and failed because a response
## contrast is a fraction of a log unit wide while its own standard error is
## about as wide -- signal and noise the same size, so reliability near zero and
## nothing to disattenuate. This file correlates ABUNDANCE against ABUNDANCE.
## Gene abundances span orders of magnitude across orthologs, measurement error
## spans a fraction of a log unit, so reliability is near one and the whole
## attenuation problem is absent. No response label enters anywhere in this file.
##
## WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN, at ortholog level, 47 paired patients, 1,320 KOs:
##
##   own coupling            rho 0.238  (IQR 0.213-0.260)
##   a stranger's metagenome rho 0.234
##   own minus stranger      +0.0062, 95% CI -0.0038 to +0.0130  (crosses zero)
##   restricted to the 200 most variable gene families
##                           +0.0333, 95% CI +0.0160 to +0.0498  (clears zero)
##
## So the layers agree about what is abundant, and that agreement is almost
## entirely GENERIC -- a stranger's metagenome predicts your proteome nearly as
## well as your own. The patient-specific part only becomes visible where gene
## content actually varies between people.
##
## THE HYPOTHESIS THIS TESTS. Summing orthologs into pathways averages
## measurement noise down, the same way restricting to the 200 most variable
## families did, but without selecting on variability. If the patient-specific
## component is real and merely buried in per-ortholog noise, aggregation should
## surface it. If the advantage stays at zero at every resolution, that is a
## stronger version of the current claim than the per-ortholog result alone.
##
## Either answer is publishable and neither depends on a response label.
##
## SIMULATED FIRST, so the expectation is on the record before the run. With a
## generic shared component plus a patient-specific one of strength `ind`,
## 1,320 orthologs, 47 patients, and 70 pathways of 19 members each:
##
##   ind = 0.00   ortholog delta -0.0005   pathway delta -0.0023
##   ind = 0.10   ortholog delta +0.0067   pathway delta +0.0105
##   ind = 0.30   ortholog delta +0.0257   pathway delta +0.0285
##
## Two things follow. Aggregation does NOT manufacture an advantage where there
## is none -- the null row stays at zero, so a positive pathway result would not
## be an artefact of summing. And the amplification is real but modest, about
## 1.5x at the weak end and nothing at the strong end. (The absolute coupling
## levels in that simulation are not matched to this data, which sits at 0.238;
## only the direction and ratio of the deltas carry over.)
##
## RUN 9 OCTOBER 2026, and the pathway arm came back a clean null. Observed at
## 59 pathways: own coupling 0.677, a stranger's 0.670, paired delta -0.0043
## (95% CI -0.0179 to +0.0040), own beating stranger in 22 of 47 patients. The
## reference distributions, 40 simulated replicates each at this resolution:
##
##   ind = 0.00   delta -0.0006  (central 95% -0.0143 to +0.0111)  own wins 49%
##   ind = 0.10   delta +0.0124  (central 95% -0.0062 to +0.0297)  own wins 60%
##
## The observation sits on the null row -- mid-distribution there, and around
## the 3rd percentile of the weak-alternative row. So the data favour no
## patient-specific coupling at pathway level over even a weak one. Note also
## that aggregation raised the GENERIC agreement from 0.238 to 0.677 while the
## patient-specific part went to zero: it is not that the assays are too noisy
## to couple.
##
## SO THE HONEST EXPECTATION. The ortholog delta is +0.0062 with an interval of
## -0.0038 to +0.0130. A 1.5x amplification puts the pathway delta near +0.009,
## while the interval will WIDEN, because each patient's rho will rest on ~70
## points instead of 1,320. The likeliest outcome is a slightly higher centre
## inside a slightly wider interval that still includes zero -- which is the
## "holds at two resolutions, and the second one did not select on variability"
## result, and is worth having. A clear positive is possible and would be the
## more interesting outcome. A clear negative is not a plausible outcome of this
## design and should be treated as a bug if it appears.
##
## WHY ZEROS ARE NOT POISON HERE, unlike in B31. There, each feature was logged
## individually and an undetected feature became a sentinel with a huge apparent
## effect and a tiny standard error. Here the operation is a SUM, and an
## undetected member contributes zero to a sum, which is simply correct. The
## pathway total is a real quantity whether or not every member was seen.
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(dplyr); library(tibble) })
`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a)) b else a

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## ko_pathways(): KEGG pathway memberships over ORTHOLOGS
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## v17 defines its KEGG pathway sets over PROTEINS (`sets$KEGGpath`, 79 of them,
## from eggNOG's KEGG_Pathway column on the Pittsburgh discovery universe). Both
## layers have to be scored on the same index, and the metagenome has no protein
## identifiers, so the memberships are projected into ortholog space through
## annot_new$ko_primary -- the same bridge used wherever the two layers or the
## two cohorts meet.
##
## The floor is deliberately low (5). A pathway's job here is to average noise
## out of a sum, and a five-member sum already does some of that; the ten-member
## floor in B33 existed because fgsea needs it, and fgsea is not used here.
##
## PATHWAYS OVERLAP -- an ortholog sits in several maps -- so they are not
## independent. For this statistic that matters much less than it did in B33:
## own and mismatched coupling are computed over the SAME index set, so the
## overlap affects both identically and cancels in the difference. It does limit
## how precisely each patient's rho is estimated, which is reported.
ko_pathways <- function(path_sets, annot = annot_new, universe = NULL,
                        min_ko = 5) {
  stopifnot(all(c("protein", "ko_primary") %in% names(annot)))
  ## SAY WHAT ARRIVED. The first run of this got an empty list -- v17 builds
  ## `sets` inside a local({...}) block, so sets$KEGGpath is NULL in a live
  ## session -- and the function went on to compute min() of nothing and died
  ## on a format string instead of saying so.
  if (!length(path_sets))
    stop("ko_pathways(): `path_sets` is empty or NULL.\n",
         "  v17 builds `sets` inside local({...}), so sets$KEGGpath does not\n",
         "  survive into the session. The saved copy does -- see B35:\n",
         "    source('B35_full_space_sets.R')\n",
         "    SF <- load_full_space()\n",
         "    kp <- SF[startsWith(names(SF), 'KEGGpath:')]   # 79 maps\n",
         "    res <- b36(kp, MP, G, pat, kos)",
         call. = FALSE)
  if (!is.list(path_sets) || is.null(names(path_sets)))
    stop("ko_pathways(): `path_sets` must be a NAMED list of protein-id vectors",
         call. = FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("ko_pathways: %d sets in, median %.0f proteins (e.g. %s)\n",
              length(path_sets), median(lengths(path_sets)),
              paste(head(names(path_sets), 2), collapse = ", ")))
  a <- annot |> filter(!is.na(ko_primary), ko_primary != "", !is.na(protein)) |>
    distinct(protein, ko_primary)
  dup <- unique(a$protein[duplicated(a$protein)])
  if (length(dup))
    stop(sprintf("ko_pathways: %d proteins carry more than one ko_primary (e.g. %s)",
                 length(dup), paste(head(dup, 3), collapse = ", ")), call. = FALSE)
  map <- setNames(a$ko_primary, a$protein)

  out <- lapply(path_sets, function(p) {
    k <- unique(unname(map[intersect(p, names(map))]))
    k <- k[!is.na(k)]
    if (!is.null(universe)) k <- intersect(k, universe)
    k
  })
  keep <- lengths(out) >= min_ko
  cat(sprintf("  %d of %d survive >= %d orthologs in the shared universe\n",
              sum(keep), length(path_sets), min_ko))
  if (!sum(keep)) {
    hit <- mean(unlist(path_sets) %in% names(map))
    stop(sprintf(paste0("ko_pathways(): no pathway survives. %.0f%% of the set",
                        " members are found in\n  annot_new$protein, so the",
                        " problem is %s."),
                 100 * hit,
                 if (hit < 0.1) paste("an identifier mismatch -- these are not",
                                      "the protein ids annot_new uses")
                 else "the size floor, or the shared ortholog universe"),
         call. = FALSE)
  }
  cat(sprintf("  median %.0f orthologs per surviving pathway (range %.0f-%.0f)\n",
              median(lengths(out[keep])), min(lengths(out[keep])),
              max(lengths(out[keep]))))
  ov <- mean(table(unlist(out[keep])) > 1)
  cat(sprintf("  %.0f%% of orthologs appear in more than one pathway\n", 100 * ov))
  out[keep]
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## aggregate_layer(): orthologs -> pathway sums, one layer, one sample set
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
aggregate_layer <- function(M, sets, samples, lab = "") {
  X <- as.matrix(M[, samples, drop = FALSE])
  X[!is.finite(X)] <- 0                     # a sum treats unobserved as zero
  P <- t(vapply(sets, function(k) {
    kk <- intersect(k, rownames(X))
    if (!length(kk)) rep(NA_real_, ncol(X)) else colSums(X[kk, , drop = FALSE])
  }, numeric(ncol(X))))
  dimnames(P) <- list(names(sets), samples)
  ok <- rowSums(is.finite(P)) == ncol(P) & apply(P, 1, function(z) sum(z > 0) > 0)
  if (nchar(lab))
    cat(sprintf("  %s: %d of %d pathways scored in all %d samples\n",
                lab, sum(ok), nrow(P), ncol(P)))
  P[ok, , drop = FALSE]
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## top_variable(): the "most variable gene families" arm, without the zero trap
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## MY FIRST VERSION OF THIS WAS WRONG and it is worth recording why, because it
## is the same mistake that produced B31's impossible rho of -0.370. Ranking
## orthologs by sd(log(cpm + 1e-9)) does not rank them by variability -- it
## ranks them by HOW MANY ZEROS THEY HAVE, because every zero becomes -20.7 and
## a single one of those dominates a standard deviation computed over 47
## numbers near zero.
##
## MY SECOND VERSION WAS ALSO WRONG, differently, and that is the more useful
## record. It restricted to orthologs present in EVERY patient and ranked them
## by sd(log(.)). It ran, it produced 200 features, and it gave an own coupling
## of 0.050 against 0.238 across all orthologs -- selecting the most variable
## features made the coupling five times WORSE, which is backwards and was the
## tell. Taking log of a CPM near zero sends it far negative, so sd(log(.))
## still ranks by proximity to the detection floor; the zero trap had been
## narrowed, not removed.
##
## v17 computes this in the A2 chunk as:
##     Gp   <- G[kos, pat$bio]                 # metagenome, KOs x patients
##     pres <- rowMeans(Gp > 0)
##     core <- names(pres)[pres >= 0.9]        # present in >= 90% of patients
##     sd_core <- apply(log1p(Gp[core, ]), 1, sd)
## Two differences from my version, both of which move the ranking:
##   log1p, not log -- log1p(x) ~ x near zero, so a low-abundance ortholog has
##     small variance instead of enormous variance. This is the one that
##     matters.
##   presence >= 0.9, not 1.0 -- a wider core, and not the same 200 features.
## This function now reproduces that definition. Passing the session's own
## sd_core still takes precedence, for when it exists.
##
## VERIFIED 10 Oct against the live session: the fallback selects 856 core
## orthologs -- the same count v17 records in its expected-values comment --
## and its top 200 are identical to head(sort(sd_core, decreasing = TRUE), 200),
## all 200 of 200. So the arm reproduces the paper's +0.0333 (p 0.00028, 34/47)
## with or without sd_core in the session, and this script no longer depends on
## an object that v17 builds inside local({...}) and does not export.
top_variable <- function(X, n = 200, sd_core = NULL, min_prev = 0.9) {
  if (!is.null(sd_core)) {
    k <- intersect(names(sort(sd_core, decreasing = TRUE)), rownames(X))
    cat(sprintf("  using the session's own sd_core (%d orthologs ranked)\n", length(k)))
    return(head(k, n))
  }
  pres <- rowMeans(X > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  core <- names(pres)[!is.na(pres) & pres >= min_prev]
  if (length(core) < n)
    stop(sprintf(paste("top_variable: only %d orthologs are present in >= %.0f%% of",
                       "patients, fewer than the %d requested."),
                 length(core), 100 * min_prev, n), call. = FALSE)
  sdv <- apply(log1p(X[core, , drop = FALSE]), 1, sd)
  cat(sprintf(paste0("  %d core orthologs (present in >= %.0f%% of patients) ranked by",
                     " sd(log1p), as v17 does; taking %d\n"),
              length(core), 100 * min_prev, min(n, length(sdv))))
  head(names(sort(sdv, decreasing = TRUE)), n)
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## couple(): the own-versus-stranger statistic, at whatever resolution
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Exactly the structure the ortholog-level analysis uses: build the full
## proteome-by-metagenome coupling matrix, read own coupling off the diagonal,
## take each patient's median against every OTHER patient's metagenome as the
## matched control, and report the difference.
##
## ONE NOTE ON THE EXISTING CODE, which this reproduces rather than changes: the
## ortholog version computes Spearman on log(x + EPS). Spearman is a rank
## correlation and the log is monotone, so the transform and the pseudocount
## have no effect on the result whatsoever. They are harmless and they are also
## doing nothing. Kept here only so the reproduction is exact; `method` can be
## set to "pearson", where the log stops being cosmetic and starts mattering.
## `bio_col` names the metagenome identifier column, because the two cohorts
## spell it differently: Pittsburgh's pairing table calls it `bio`, Sheba's
## (B12's `pairs`) calls it `mg`. Hard-coding "bio" would have silently indexed
## a NULL for Sheba, and pat$bio on a table without that column returns NULL
## rather than erroring -- so the stopifnot below would have passed on nothing.
couple <- function(Y, X, pat, eps = 1e-9, method = c("spearman", "pearson"),
                   detected_only = TRUE, bio_col = "bio") {
  method <- match.arg(method)
  n <- nrow(pat)
  if (!all(c("sample", bio_col) %in% names(pat)))
    stop(sprintf("couple(): pairing table needs `sample` and `%s`; it has %s",
                 bio_col, paste(names(pat), collapse = ", ")), call. = FALSE)
  bio <- as.character(pat[[bio_col]])
  stopifnot(all(pat$sample %in% colnames(Y)), all(bio %in% colnames(X)))
  idx <- intersect(rownames(Y), rownames(X))
  Y <- Y[idx, pat$sample, drop = FALSE]; X <- X[idx, bio, drop = FALSE]

  one <- function(i, j) {
    y <- Y[, i]; x <- X[, j]
    k <- if (detected_only) y > 0 else rep(TRUE, length(y))
    k <- k & is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
    if (sum(k) < 10) return(NA_real_)
    suppressWarnings(cor(log(y[k] + eps), log(x[k] + eps), method = method))
  }
  ## With Spearman the log and the pseudocount are inert. With Pearson they are
  ## not: a zero becomes log(eps), which for eps = 1e-9 is -20.7 -- a sentinel
  ## far below every real value, and a handful of them would set the
  ## correlation. Refuse rather than return a plausible number.
  if (method == "pearson" && any(X[is.finite(X)] <= 0))
    stop("couple(): method = 'pearson' with zeros present. log(0 + eps) is a\n",
         "  sentinel, not a small value, and it would drive the correlation.\n",
         "  Either keep Spearman, or restrict to features with no zeros.",
         call. = FALSE)
  K <- outer(seq_len(n), seq_len(n), Vectorize(one))
  own <- diag(K)
  mis <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) median(K[i, -i], na.rm = TRUE), 0)
  rk  <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) mean(K[i, -i] >= own[i], na.rm = TRUE), 0)
  tibble(sample = pat$sample, bio = pat$bio,
         own = own, mismatched = mis, delta = own - mis, p_own = rk) |>
    structure(n_features = length(idx))
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## report_couple(): test and interval, both, because the paper reports both
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
report_couple <- function(cpl, lab, B = 4000, seed = 1) {
  d <- cpl$delta[is.finite(cpl$delta)]
  ## conf.int = TRUE ADDED 11 Oct 2026. This call already supplied the P the
  ## paper quotes; it was simply not asked for the matching location estimate,
  ## so a bootstrap of the MEDIAN was used for the interval instead. Those are
  ## two different quantities, and in the ulcerative-colitis cohort they differ
  ## by a factor of two. One call now gives estimate, interval and P together,
  ## which is the only way they cannot drift apart.
  w <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(cpl$own, cpl$mismatched, paired = TRUE,
                                    conf.int = TRUE))
  ## The bootstrap below uses `d`, which drops non-finite deltas; the paired
  ## call above drops incomplete pairs. Normally the same rows -- but if they
  ## are not, the interval and the P describe different subsets, so say so.
  n_paired <- sum(is.finite(cpl$own) & is.finite(cpl$mismatched))
  if (n_paired != length(d))
    cat(sprintf("  NOTE: %d finite deltas but %d complete pairs; the bootstrap and\n        the Wilcoxon interval are not over the same subjects.\n",
                length(d), n_paired))
  set.seed(seed)
  bs <- replicate(B, median(sample(d, length(d), replace = TRUE)))
  ci <- unname(quantile(bs, c(0.025, 0.975)))
  cat(sprintf("\n%s  (%d patients, %d features)\n", lab, nrow(cpl),
              attr(cpl, "n_features")))
  cat(sprintf("  own coupling        rho %+.3f (IQR %+.3f to %+.3f)\n",
              median(cpl$own, na.rm = TRUE),
              quantile(cpl$own, .25, na.rm = TRUE),
              quantile(cpl$own, .75, na.rm = TRUE)))
  cat(sprintf("  a stranger's        rho %+.3f\n", median(cpl$mismatched, na.rm = TRUE)))
  ## THE TWO ROWS ABOVE DO NOT SUBTRACT TO THE ROW BELOW, and the first version
  ## of this printout left that looking like a contradiction. The rows above are
  ## the median own coupling and the median mismatched coupling, each taken
  ## across patients. The row below is the median of the per-patient
  ## DIFFERENCES, which is the paired statistic and is not the difference of two
  ## medians. On the pathway run they came out +0.007 and -0.0043 respectively.
  ## The paired figure is the one to quote; the other two are for scale.
  cat(sprintf("  own minus stranger  %+.4f, 95%% CI %+.4f to %+.4f  (%s zero)\n",
              median(d), ci[1], ci[2],
              if (ci[1] > 0 || ci[2] < 0) "excludes" else "includes"))
  cat(sprintf("    (paired median of per-patient differences; the two rows above\n     are medians of each side and do not subtract to it -- %+.4f does not\n     equal %+.4f)\n",
              median(cpl$own, na.rm = TRUE) - median(cpl$mismatched, na.rm = TRUE),
              median(d)))
  cat(sprintf("  own minus stranger  %+.4f, 95%% CI %+.4f to %+.4f  (Hodges-Lehmann;\n                      this is the one the main text reports)\n",
              unname(w$estimate), w$conf.int[1], w$conf.int[2]))
  cat(sprintf("  own > stranger in %d of %d; paired Wilcoxon p = %.3g; own-p < 0.05 in %d\n",
              sum(d > 0), length(d), w$p.value, sum(cpl$p_own < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)))
  invisible(c(own = median(cpl$own, na.rm = TRUE),
              mis = median(cpl$mismatched, na.rm = TRUE),
              delta = median(d), lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2], p = w$p.value,
              hl = unname(w$estimate), hl_lo = w$conf.int[1],
              hl_hi = w$conf.int[2]))
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## b36(): run it at both resolutions, ortholog level first as the control
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## THE ORTHOLOG ROW IS NOT DECORATION. If this code does not reproduce the
## recorded 0.238 / 0.234 / +0.0062 / 27 of 47, then its pathway number is not
## comparable with anything in the paper and must not be reported. The function
## checks that itself and says so.
## `record` is the Pittsburgh reproduction target. It is an argument rather than
## a constant because the check is a statement about ONE cohort's recorded
## numbers, and firing it on Sheba would report a spurious failure. Pass NULL
## for any cohort that has no record to reproduce.
b36 <- function(path_sets, MP, G, pat, kos, annot = annot_new,
                min_ko = 5, top_var = 200, sd_core = NULL, bio_col = "bio",
                record = c(own = 0.238, mis = 0.234, delta = 0.0062),
                record_top = 0.0333, cohort = "Pittsburgh") {
  ## Pick up the session's own sd_core unless one was passed. The default
  ## cannot be written as `sd_core = if (exists("sd_core")) sd_core else NULL`:
  ## a default argument is evaluated inside the function, where `sd_core` is
  ## the formal itself, so that expression self-references and R raises
  ## "promise already under evaluation". Resolve it from the global
  ## environment explicitly instead.
  ##
  ## This is why the most-variable arm reported DIFFERS on every run so far:
  ## the vector was sitting in the session and nothing fetched it.
  if (is.null(sd_core) && exists("sd_core", envir = globalenv())) {
    sd_core <- get("sd_core", envir = globalenv())
    cat("using the session's sd_core (", length(sd_core),
        " orthologs) for the most-variable arm\n", sep = "")
  }

  cat("--- memberships ---------------------------------------------------\n")
  sets <- ko_pathways(path_sets, annot, universe = kos, min_ko = min_ko)
  if (length(sets) < 20)
    warning(sprintf(paste("only %d pathways survive; each patient's rho rests on",
                          "that many points, so the couplings themselves will be",
                          "noisy even though their difference is paired."),
                    length(sets)), call. = FALSE)

  cat("\n--- ortholog level ------------------------------------------------\n")
  bio <- as.character(pat[[bio_col]])
  Y <- as.matrix(MP[kos, pat$sample, drop = FALSE])
  X <- as.matrix(G[kos,  bio,        drop = FALSE])
  c_ko <- couple(Y, X, pat, bio_col = bio_col)
  r_ko <- report_couple(c_ko, sprintf("orthologs, all %d", length(kos)))
  if (!is.null(record)) {
    off <- abs(r_ko[c("own", "mis", "delta")] - record[c("own", "mis", "delta")])
    cat(sprintf("  against the record (%.3f / %.3f / %+.4f): %s\n",
                record[["own"]], record[["mis"]], record[["delta"]],
                if (all(off < c(0.005, 0.005, 0.0015))) "REPRODUCED"
                else sprintf("DIFFERS by %.3f / %.3f / %.4f -- do not report the pathway row until this is understood",
                             off[1], off[2], off[3])))
  } else cat("  no recorded value for this cohort; nothing to reproduce against\n")

  cat("\n--- the most variable orthologs, the paper's other arm -------------\n")
  ## Survivable. On a smaller cohort there may be fewer core orthologs than
  ## `top_var`, and this arm failing must not abort the run before the pathway
  ## row, which is the reason the function was called.
  r_top <- tryCatch({
    topk <- top_variable(X, top_var, sd_core = sd_core)
    c_top <- couple(Y[topk, , drop = FALSE], X[topk, , drop = FALSE], pat,
                    bio_col = bio_col)
    rt <- report_couple(c_top, sprintf("orthologs, %d most variable", length(topk)))
    ## WITHOUT A RECORD, THIS ARM IS A RECOMPUTATION AND NOT THE PAPER'S NUMBER.
    ## Measured 11 Oct 2026: for Sheba this arm gives a median of +0.0137 and a
    ## Hodges-Lehmann estimate of +0.0094, where B14 reports -0.0061 and -0.0136.
    ## They are not the same quantity. B14 does not compute Sheba's most-variable
    ## arm at all -- its line `dS_top <- b12$own_top - b12$mis_top` reads B12's
    ## ARCHIVED values, which are what the pre-specified replication recorded and
    ## what the paper quotes. This file instead ranks Sheba's own core set (612
    ## orthologs here against Pittsburgh's 856), so it selects a different 200.
    ##
    ## Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. The archived one is the
    ## paper's, because freezing the Sheba arm before it was scored is the whole
    ## point of that cohort. The recomputation is a useful cross-check and must
    ## not be quoted as the result -- hence this notice rather than a silent row.
    ##
    ## It reaches nothing downstream: b36_save() writes only the `pathways` row.
    if (is.null(record_top))
      cat("  NOT THE PAPER'S NUMBER for this cohort: no archived value was passed,\n",
          "  so this arm ranks this cohort's own core set rather than reproducing\n",
          "  the frozen one. B14 reports the archived arm; quote that. See the\n",
          "  comment above this message in B36_pathway_coupling.R.\n", sep = "")
    if (!is.null(record_top))
      cat(sprintf("  against the record (%+.4f): %s\n", record_top,
                  if (abs(rt[["delta"]] - record_top) < 0.004) "REPRODUCED"
                  else sprintf(paste0("DIFFERS (%+.4f). %s"), rt[["delta"]],
                    if (is.null(sd_core))
                      paste("sd_core was neither passed nor found in the session, so this",
                            "arm ranked variability its own way and is NOT a reproduction",
                            "of the paper's arm. The ortholog arm above is the one that",
                            "validates this script.")
                    else
                      paste("sd_core WAS used, so the ranking is the paper's and this",
                            "difference is real. Do not dismiss it."))))
    rt
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat("  SKIPPED: ", conditionMessage(e), "\n", sep = "")
    NULL
  })

  cat("\n--- pathway level, the new question --------------------------------\n")
  Pm <- aggregate_layer(MP, sets, pat$sample, "proteome")
  Pg <- aggregate_layer(G,  sets, bio,         "metagenome")
  ## detected_only is FALSE here: a pathway sum is positive for nearly every
  ## pathway, so the ortholog-level "keep what the proteome detected" filter is
  ## vacuous at this resolution, and leaving it on would silently mean something
  ## different from what it means above.
  c_pw <- couple(Pm, Pg, pat, detected_only = FALSE, bio_col = bio_col)
  r_pw <- report_couple(c_pw, sprintf("pathways, %d", nrow(Pm)))

  cat("\n--- the three resolutions together ---------------------------------\n")
  tab <- bind_rows(
    tibble(resolution = "orthologs, all",     !!!as.list(r_ko)),
    if (!is.null(r_top))
      tibble(resolution = "orthologs, top var", !!!as.list(r_top)),
    tibble(resolution = "pathways",           !!!as.list(r_pw))) |>
    mutate(across(c(own, mis), ~ round(., 3)),
           across(c(delta, lo, hi), ~ round(., 4)))
  print(as.data.frame(tab))

  cat("\nREADING. The paper's claim is that capacity information is generic and\n",
      "shared rather than individual and quantitative. If the pathway delta is\n",
      "also at zero, that claim now holds at two resolutions and under an\n",
      "aggregation that does NOT select on variability -- which is the stronger\n",
      "statement, because the top-200 arm could always be answered with 'you\n",
      "chose the features where it would show'. If instead the pathway delta\n",
      "clears zero, the patient-specific component is real and was buried in\n",
      "per-ortholog noise; report it as a magnitude and not as a test, since the\n",
      "interesting thing is how small it is.\n", sep = "")
  invisible(list(table = tab, ko = c_ko, pathway = c_pw, sets = sets,
                 cohort = cohort))
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## b36_save(): the pathway arm, in the shape p5e already reads
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Figure S3A ("How large can a patient's own-metagenome advantage be?") reads
## B14's table: cohort, arm, n, median, lo, hi, own_coupling, excludes_zero.
## Writing the pathway arm in that exact shape means the panel binds it in
## without knowing anything about this file, and still renders if B36 never ran.
##
## `cohort` is an argument rather than hard-coded "Pittsburgh" so the same call
## adds a Sheba row once that cohort's MP / G / pat equivalents are passed to
## b36(). Nothing here is Pittsburgh-specific.
b36_save <- function(res, cohort = res$cohort %||% "Pittsburgh",
                     arm = "pathways",
                     out_dir = paths$out_dir) {
  r <- res$table |> filter(resolution == "pathways")
  if (!nrow(r)) stop("b36_save(): no pathway row in res$table", call. = FALSE)
  ## `n` is PATIENTS, matching B14's column -- and nrow() of a per-patient
  ## tibble is that. `n_features` is PATHWAYS and nrow() is not: the first
  ## version used it for both and recorded 47 pathways where there are 59.
  ## couple() attaches the feature count as an attribute; read it there.
  nf <- attr(res$pathway, "n_features")
  ## hl/hl_lo/hl_hi ADDED 11 Oct 2026 -- these are the columns figures_v2.Rmd's
  ## S3A panel looks for. Without them it falls back to the median columns and
  ## says so on its axis, so a stale B36 cannot silently put a median in a
  ## figure whose caption and text quote Hodges-Lehmann.
  has_hl <- all(c("hl", "hl_lo", "hl_hi") %in% names(r))
  if (!has_hl)
    stop("b36_save(): res$table carries no hl columns. This res came from a ",
         "run before 11 Oct; re-run b36() so report_couple() supplies them.",
         call. = FALSE)
  row <- tibble(cohort = cohort, arm = arm, n = nrow(res$pathway),
                median = r$delta[1], lo = r$lo[1], hi = r$hi[1],
                hl = r$hl[1], hl_lo = r$hl_lo[1], hl_hi = r$hl_hi[1],
                own_coupling = r$own[1],
                excludes_zero = r$lo[1] > 0 | r$hi[1] < 0,
                hl_excludes_zero = r$hl_lo[1] > 0 | r$hl_hi[1] < 0,
                n_features = if (is.null(nf)) NA_integer_ else as.integer(nf))
  od <- file.path(out_dir, "B36_pathway_coupling")
  dir.create(od, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  f <- file.path(od, "magnitude.rds")
  ## Accumulate rather than overwrite, so a Sheba run added later joins the
  ## Pittsburgh one instead of replacing it.
  if (file.exists(f)) {
    old <- readRDS(f)
    row <- bind_rows(old |> filter(!(cohort == !!cohort & arm == !!arm)), row)
  }
  saveRDS(row, f)
  cat(sprintf("b36_save: %d row(s) -> %s\n", nrow(row), f))
  print(as.data.frame(row))
  invisible(row)
}

cat("B36 loaded.\n\n",
    "PITTSBURGH. v17 builds `sets` inside local({...}), so sets$KEGGpath is not\n",
    "in a live session; take the saved copy, which B35 loads:\n\n",
    "  source('B35_full_space_sets.R'); source('B36_pathway_coupling.R')\n",
    "  SF  <- load_full_space()\n",
    "  kp  <- SF[startsWith(names(SF), 'KEGGpath:')]       # the 79 KEGG maps\n",
    "  res <- b36(kp, MP, G, pat, kos)\n",
    "  b36_save(res)\n\n",
    "SHEBA. The objects are B12's, and its pairing table spells the metagenome\n",
    "column `mg` where Pittsburgh's spells it `bio`:\n\n",
    "  res_s <- b36(kp, MPs, KO, pairs, kos_s, bio_col = 'mg',\n",
    "               record = NULL, record_top = NULL, cohort = 'Sheba')\n",
    "  b36_save(res_s)\n\n",
    "  MPs   1201 x 35  protein shares per ortholog   (B12: sweep(Msum, 2, colSums))\n",
    "  KO    5548 x 46  the Sheba metagenome KO table\n",
    "  kos_s 1116       intersect(rownames(MPs), rownames(KO))\n",
    "  pairs 30 x 9     sample = proteome, mg = metagenome\n\n",
    "WHY SHEBA USES THE SAME `kp`, which is a real design choice and not laziness.\n",
    "A KEGG map's membership is a property of KEGG, not of a cohort. Passing\n",
    "Pittsburgh's protein sets and intersecting the projection with kos_s gives\n",
    "the KO IMAGE of each map restricted to what Sheba measured, so the two\n",
    "cohorts get identical map definitions in ortholog space and differ only in\n",
    "coverage. v17's own sets_s would instead define each map by the proteins\n",
    "Sheba happened to detect, which mixes the definition with the detection and\n",
    "makes the two rows look comparable while measuring different things.\n",
    "  The cost, stated: an ortholog that belongs to a map, was measured in Sheba\n",
    "and never annotated in Pittsburgh is missing from the image. That is a\n",
    "coverage limit on the map definition, identical for both cohorts, which is\n",
    "the property worth having here.\n\n",
    "record = NULL on Sheba because the reproduction check is a statement about\n",
    "Pittsburgh's recorded 0.238 / 0.234 / +0.0062 and would report a spurious\n",
    "failure on any other cohort. No response label is used anywhere in this file.\n",
    sep = "")
```

## B37 — variance partition

cohort against response, on one axis

Source: `B37_variance_partition.R`

```{r B37_variance_partition, eval=FALSE}
## ============================================================================
## B37 — cohort against response, on one axis
## ============================================================================
##
## WHAT THIS IS FOR. The paper runs PERMANOVA separately within each cohort and
## reports a response R2 per arm (B15, Supplementary Figure 2a). It never puts
## cohort and response on the same axis, so a reader cannot see the thing that
## governs the whole two-centre design: site explains far more of the profile
## than response does. One picture, two bars, and the rest of the paper's
## caution about replication stops needing to be argued.
##
## THE NUMBER IS EASY TO OVERSTATE, AND THE OLD VERSION OF THIS FIGURE DID.
## It reported cohort 35.0% against response 2.2% on log2 pathway scores across
## both cohorts. The two proteomes do not measure the same feature set --
## Pittsburgh has 1,404 orthologs, Sheba 1,201 -- and a CLR with a 1e-9
## pseudocount turns every undetected ortholog into log(1e-9) = -20.7. If the
## two cohorts differ in WHICH orthologs they detect, that pattern alone
## separates them, and the cohort R2 is then partly a statement about detection
## rather than about biology.
##
## So the primary analysis here runs on orthologs detected in EVERY sample of
## both cohorts, where no pseudocount is in play, and the prevalence floor is
## swept so the dependence is visible instead of assumed. Read the sweep before
## quoting any single number: if the cohort R2 falls steeply as the floor
## rises, the headline figure was detection.
##
## No disattenuation, no cross-layer correlation, nothing from B31-B35 here.
## This is one distance matrix and a two-factor decomposition of it.
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(dplyr); library(tibble) })

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## joint_proteome(): both cohorts on one shared feature set
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## `samp` must carry sample, cohort and resp -- SAMP_PRIMARY does. Channels
## without a response label are pooled references and are dropped.
joint_proteome <- function(MP, MPs, samp, min_prev = 1.0,
                           plex_col = "Mixture") {
  need <- c("sample", "cohort", "resp")
  if (!all(need %in% names(samp)))
    stop("joint_proteome(): `samp` needs ", paste(need, collapse = ", "),
         "; it has ", paste(names(samp), collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
  shared <- intersect(rownames(MP), rownames(MPs))
  if (length(shared) < 100)
    stop(sprintf("joint_proteome(): only %d orthologs shared between the two
  matrices. Check that both are ortholog-by-sample with matching row names.",
                 length(shared)), call. = FALSE)
  M <- cbind(MP[shared, , drop = FALSE], MPs[shared, , drop = FALSE])
  d <- samp |>
    filter(sample %in% colnames(M), !is.na(resp)) |>
    distinct(sample, .keep_all = TRUE)
  M <- M[, d$sample, drop = FALSE]
  d$cohort <- droplevels(factor(d$cohort))
  d$resp   <- droplevels(factor(d$resp))
  d$plex   <- if (plex_col %in% names(d)) droplevels(factor(d[[plex_col]]))
              else droplevels(factor(d$cohort))
  if (nlevels(d$cohort) != 2)
    stop("joint_proteome(): need exactly two cohorts, found ",
         paste(levels(d$cohort), collapse = "/"), call. = FALSE)

  ## Re-close each column AFTER the feature restriction. These are shares over
  ## each cohort's own ortholog universe, and once the universe is cut to the
  ## shared set they no longer sum to one; leaving them unclosed would put a
  ## cohort-sized constant into every CLR row.
  keep <- rowMeans(M > 0, na.rm = TRUE) >= min_prev
  for (lv in levels(d$cohort)) {                       # per cohort, per floor
    i <- d$cohort == lv
    keep <- keep & rowMeans(M[, i, drop = FALSE] > 0, na.rm = TRUE) >= min_prev
  }
  M <- M[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(M) < 20)
    stop(sprintf("joint_proteome(): only %d orthologs clear a prevalence floor
  of %.2f in both cohorts. Lower min_prev deliberately and report it.",
                 nrow(M), min_prev), call. = FALSE)
  M <- sweep(M, 2, colSums(M, na.rm = TRUE), "/")
  cat(sprintf("joint_proteome: %d samples (%s), %d of %d shared orthologs at prevalence >= %.2f\n",
              ncol(M), paste(sprintf("%s=%d", levels(d$cohort), table(d$cohort)),
                             collapse = " "),
              nrow(M), length(shared), min_prev))
  cat(sprintf("  response: %s\n",
              paste(sprintf("%s %d", levels(d$resp), table(d$resp)), collapse = ", ")))
  list(M = t(M), d = d, n_shared = length(shared), min_prev = min_prev)
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## gower(): the same centring B15 uses, so the two are commensurable
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
.clr <- function(M, eps = 1e-9) { L <- log(M + eps); sweep(L, 1, rowMeans(L), "-") }
.gower <- function(D) {
  A <- -0.5 * D^2
  n <- nrow(A); J <- diag(n) - matrix(1 / n, n, n)
  J %*% A %*% J
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## partition(): marginal R2 for each term, on one distance matrix
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Distance-based redundancy analysis. For a model matrix X, column-centred,
## R2 = tr(H G) / tr(G) with H the hat matrix. The MARGINAL contribution of a
## term is R2(full) - R2(full without that term), which is what adonis2's
## by = "margin" reports and what makes "cohort 35% against response 2%"
## a fair comparison rather than an order-dependent one.
##
## ONLY THE RESPONSE TERM GETS A P-VALUE, and that is deliberate. Plex is
## nested within cohort, so there is no exchangeable unit under which cohort
## labels can be permuted -- shuffling them breaks the nesting and the
## resulting p would be a statement about the shuffle, not the data. The
## cohort R2 is a magnitude, and that is all this panel claims for it.
.r2 <- function(X, G) {
  X <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
  qrX <- qr(X); if (qrX$rank == 0) return(0)
  Q <- qr.Q(qrX)[, seq_len(qrX$rank), drop = FALSE]
  sum(diag(crossprod(Q, G) %*% Q)) / sum(diag(G))
}

partition <- function(jp, B = 999, seed = 1, eps = 1e-9) {
  M <- jp$M; d <- jp$d
  Z <- .clr(M, eps)
  D <- as.matrix(dist(Z))
  G <- .gower(D)
  mm <- function(f) model.matrix(f, d)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
  X_full <- cbind(mm(~ cohort), mm(~ resp))
  r2_full <- .r2(X_full, G)
  r2_coh  <- r2_full - .r2(mm(~ resp),   G)
  r2_res  <- r2_full - .r2(mm(~ cohort), G)

  ## response permuted WITHIN cohort and plex, which is the exchangeable unit
  set.seed(seed)
  strata <- interaction(d$cohort, d$plex, drop = TRUE)
  nul <- replicate(B, {
    rp <- d$resp
    for (lv in levels(strata)) {
      i <- which(strata == lv); if (length(i) > 1) rp[i] <- d$resp[sample(i)]
    }
    dd <- d; dd$resp <- rp
    Xr <- model.matrix(~ resp, dd)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
    .r2(cbind(mm(~ cohort), Xr), G) - .r2(mm(~ cohort), G)
  })
  p_res <- (1 + sum(nul >= r2_res)) / (1 + B)

  cat(sprintf("\npartition: %d samples, %d orthologs, prevalence floor %.2f\n",
              nrow(M), ncol(M), jp$min_prev))
  cat(sprintf("  cohort    marginal R2 %.4f  (%.1f%%)   no P: plex is nested in cohort\n",
              r2_coh, 100 * r2_coh))
  cat(sprintf("  response  marginal R2 %.4f  (%.1f%%)   P = %.4f (%d permutations within cohort x plex)\n",
              r2_res, 100 * r2_res, p_res, B))
  cat(sprintf("  together  %.4f (%.1f%%); cohort is %.1f times response\n",
              r2_full, 100 * r2_full,
              if (r2_res > 0) r2_coh / r2_res else NA_real_))
  tibble(term = c("Cohort", "Response"),
         r2 = c(r2_coh, r2_res),
         p = c(NA_real_, p_res),
         n = nrow(M), n_features = ncol(M), min_prev = jp$min_prev)
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## b37(): the sweep, then the primary
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## The sweep comes FIRST and is printed whether or not anyone asks, because the
## single number is only meaningful alongside it.
b37 <- function(MP, MPs, samp, floors = c(1.0, 0.9, 0.75, 0.5, 0.0),
                primary = 1.0, B = 999, out_dir = NULL) {
  cat("--- prevalence sweep: how much of the cohort effect is detection? ---\n")
  sw <- bind_rows(lapply(floors, function(f) {
    jp <- tryCatch(joint_proteome(MP, MPs, samp, min_prev = f),
                   error = function(e) { cat("  floor ", f, ": ",
                                             conditionMessage(e), "\n", sep = ""); NULL })
    if (is.null(jp)) return(NULL)
    p <- partition(jp, B = 99)                     # cheap for the sweep
    p$min_prev <- f; p
  }))
  if (!nrow(sw)) stop("b37(): no prevalence floor produced a usable matrix",
                      call. = FALSE)
  cat("\n--- sweep ---\n")
  print(sw |> select(min_prev, term, r2, n_features) |>
          tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = r2) |>
          mutate(ratio = Cohort / Response) |> as.data.frame())
  cat("\nREAD THIS BEFORE QUOTING A NUMBER. If Cohort falls steeply as the floor\n",
      "rises, the headline was detection and the high-floor row is the honest\n",
      "one. If it is flat, the cohort effect is in the abundances and any row\n",
      "will do -- quote the primary.\n", sep = "")

  cat("\n--- primary, prevalence floor ", primary, " ---\n", sep = "")
  res <- partition(joint_proteome(MP, MPs, samp, min_prev = primary), B = B)
  if (!is.null(out_dir)) {
    od <- file.path(out_dir, "B37_variance_partition")
    dir.create(od, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
    saveRDS(list(primary = res, sweep = sw), file.path(od, "partition.rds"))
    cat("saved -> ", file.path(od, "partition.rds"), "\n", sep = "")
  }
  invisible(list(primary = res, sweep = sw))
}

cat("B37 loaded. With v17's figure inputs in the session:\n\n",
    "  source('B37_variance_partition.R')\n",
    "  v <- b37(MP, MPs, SAMP_PRIMARY, out_dir = paths$out_dir)\n\n",
    "MP   Pittsburgh ortholog shares (1,404 x 55)\n",
    "MPs  Sheba ortholog shares      (1,201 x 35)   -- B12 builds it\n",
    "SAMP_PRIMARY  sample, cohort, resp, Mixture    (116 rows)\n\n",
    "The sweep prints first. The old version of this figure reported cohort\n",
    "35.0% against response 2.2% on all shared features with a 1e-9 pseudocount;\n",
    "if that number was detection rather than biology, the sweep says so.\n",
    sep = "")
```

## B38 — species direction

the signal partitions WITHIN a genus

Source: `B38_species_direction.R`

```{r B38_species_direction, eval=FALSE}
## ============================================================================
## B38 — the signal partitions WITHIN a genus
## ============================================================================
##
## WHAT IT ADDS. The paper shows "No single genus carries it" and compares
## within-genus against community-level effects, and stops at genus. One level
## down, the partition is sharper: among Lachnospiraceae, B. wexlerae and
## B. obeum carry the non-responder direction while B. caecimuris and B. faecis
## lean the other way. A genus is not the unit the signal lives on, and showing
## that is a stronger specificity claim than showing no genus dominates.
##
## WHERE THE DATA COME FROM. v17 exports taxonomy at phylum, family and genus
## (pep_ph, pep_fa, pep_g) and NOT at species, but it builds all three with one
## function from one cache, so species needs no new annotation -- only the same
## call at a fourth rank:
##
##     pep_tax2(OP, "pitt",  "species_name")
##     pep_tax2(OS, "sheba", "species_name")
##
## This file rebuilds that locally rather than depending on pep_tax2 still
## being in scope, and checks the cache actually carries a species column
## before doing anything else.
##
## THE SIGN CONVENTION IS ANCHORED, NOT ASSUMED. Whether a positive statistic
## means non-responder-up depends on how the contrast was formed, and getting
## it backwards would invert every bar while looking perfectly reasonable. So
## the direction is calibrated against the chaperone set, which this paper
## establishes is elevated in non-responders: if the chaperones come out R-up,
## the convention is wrong and the script says so and stops.
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(dplyr); library(tibble) })

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## pep_species(): PSM row -> species, the way v17 builds its other ranks
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
pep_species <- function(lca, O, cohort, rank_col = "species_name") {
  if (!is.data.frame(lca))
    stop("pep_species(): `lca` must be the Unipept cache data frame ",
         "(v17 calls it lca_all2)", call. = FALSE)
  if (!rank_col %in% names(lca))
    stop(sprintf(paste0("pep_species(): the cache has no `%s` column. It has:",
                        "\n  %s\nUnipept returns species_name when the LCA",
                        " resolves that far; if this cache was fetched at a",
                        " coarser rank it has to be re-fetched."),
                 rank_col, paste(names(lca), collapse = ", ")), call. = FALSE)
  if (is.null(O$rd$seq) || is.null(O$rd$Protein))
    stop("pep_species(): `O$rd` needs `seq` and `Protein`", call. = FALSE)
  r <- lca |> filter(cohort == !!cohort) |>
    select(seq = peptide, tax = all_of(rank_col)) |>
    mutate(tax = na_if(trimws(tax), "")) |>
    filter(!is.na(tax)) |> distinct(seq, .keep_all = TRUE)
  out <- tibble(row = seq_len(nrow(O$a)), seq = O$rd$seq,
                Protein = O$rd$Protein) |> inner_join(r, by = "seq")
  cat(sprintf("pep_species[%s]: %d of %d PSM rows resolve to species (%.1f%%)\n",
              cohort, nrow(out), nrow(O$a), 100 * nrow(out) / nrow(O$a)))
  out
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## protein_species(): one species per protein, with the ambiguity reported
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## A protein's PSMs can resolve to several species. Taking the modal one
## silently would hide how often that choice was close; `purity_min` makes it
## a decision. Proteins below the threshold are dropped, not reassigned.
protein_species <- function(ps, purity_min = 0.6) {
  g <- ps |> count(Protein, tax, name = "n") |>
    group_by(Protein) |>
    mutate(purity = n / sum(n)) |>
    slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    ungroup()
  kept <- g |> filter(purity >= purity_min)
  cat(sprintf("  %d proteins with a species call; %d at purity >= %.2f (median purity %.2f)\n",
              nrow(g), nrow(kept), purity_min, median(g$purity)))
  kept |> transmute(Protein, species = tax, purity)
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## direction_counts(): per species, how many proteins move each way
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## `stat` is a NAMED protein-level statistic. `nr_up_sign` says which sign
## means non-responder-up; it is checked against the chaperone set below
## rather than trusted.
direction_counts <- function(prot_sp, stat, nr_up_sign = -1, min_n = 3,
                             genera = NULL, p0 = NULL) {
  s <- stat[intersect(names(stat), prot_sp$Protein)]
  s <- s[is.finite(s) & s != 0]
  d <- prot_sp |> filter(Protein %in% names(s)) |>
    mutate(v = unname(s[Protein]),
           direction = ifelse(sign(v) == nr_up_sign, "NR-up", "R-up"),
           genus = sub(" .*$", "", species))
  ## THE NULL IS THE BACKGROUND RATE, NOT 50:50, and the first version of this
  ## function got that wrong. binom.test(n_NRup, n_total) asks whether a species
  ## departs from an even split -- but if the statistic is globally skewed, every
  ## species inherits the skew and the test reports it as a finding. The first
  ## run put B. wexlerae at 111:139 with p = 0.088 against 0.5; if the
  ## background rate is near 44% that species is exactly average and the p
  ## means nothing. The reference is the rate across ALL species-assigned
  ## proteins, so the question becomes "does this species differ from the rest
  ## of the assigned proteome", which is the question the panel is making.
  bg <- mean(d$direction == "NR-up")
  p0 <- if (is.null(p0)) bg else p0
  cat(sprintf("  background: %.1f%% of %d species-assigned proteins read NR-up -- used as the null
",
              100 * bg, nrow(d)))
  if (abs(bg - 0.5) > 0.05)
    cat(sprintf("    (a 50:50 null would have been wrong by %.0f percentage points here)\n",
                100 * abs(bg - 0.5)))
  if (!is.null(genera)) d <- d |> filter(genus %in% genera)
  out <- d |> group_by(genus, species) |>
    summarise(n_total = n(), n_NRup = sum(direction == "NR-up"),
              n_Rup = sum(direction == "R-up"), .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(n_total >= min_n) |>
    rowwise() |>
    mutate(sign_p = binom.test(n_NRup, n_total, p = p0)$p.value,
           pct_NRup = 100 * n_NRup / n_total) |>
    ungroup()
  ## Corrected within the family of species actually displayed. With a few
  ## dozen species and a handful of proteins each, almost nothing survives --
  ## which is the honest state of this panel and should be visible in it
  ## rather than discovered by a reader.
```
